subject: Hardware mapping for BlueWave Dedicated: H100 / A100 / L4 tradeoffs
messages:

Subject: Dedicated capacity: mapping recommendations for our workload

Hi Soojin,

Thanks again for the demo last week. Our infra/ML teams dug into the perf numbers you shared and want a short note describing how you’d map BlueWave’s workload to hardware for a Dedicated deployment. High-level points we need:
- Which GPU(s) to reserve for our baseline: H100, A100, L4 — and why.
- When to prefer H100 vs A100 vs L4 (memory, throughput, long-context).
- How to handle fallbacks and burst capacity (cost containment + reliability).
- Any recommended quantization/precision/instance choices that materially change cost estimates.

Context: our main usage is multi-user RAG assistants (avg payloads 2–4k tokens, ~60% of requests are embedding/semantic search; 40% generation with occasional up to 64k contexts for specialized accounts). Target: 99th percentile latency < 300ms for interactive queries and predictable throughput for overnight batches.

Can you put together something concise we can circulate with procurement? We’re trying to finalize the reserved tier in the next two weeks.

Best,
Marta

Subject: Re: Dedicated capacity: mapping recommendations for our workload

Marta — thanks for the clear ask. I put a short fit/decision summary below and attached a spreadsheet with cost sensitivity and run-rate projections (bluewave-hw-fit-analysis.xlsx). Quick TL;DR up top, followed by rationale and a suggested mapping for baseline vs burst.

TL;DR recommendation:
- Baseline: A100 (80GB) pool for mixed generation and throughput-heavy traffic — gives predictable batching and cost-efficiency for the 2–4k token common case.
- Long-context, high-quality gen (64k contexts / research accounts): H100 nodes in a smaller, pinned pool (can be reserved but smaller commit) to avoid latency blowups and to support models with very large KV cache and fp16 workloads.
- Cost-sensitive endpoints and embedding-only traffic: L4 as the economical scale-out layer for embeddings and low-latency small-gen paths. L4 works well for short-context chat and high-concurrency embedding calls.

Rationale / details:
- Memory vs throughput: H100 + 80GB+ configurations excel where KV cache needs are large (very long context) and for models that benefit from Tensor Cores at FP16/FP8. A100 (80GB) is the workhorse for many open models at 8–32k contexts with robust batching; it typically gives better tokens/sec per dollar for mid-length sequences because it can be packed more efficiently. L4 is specialized for cost-per-embedding and low-latency small generation (lower VRAM but high efficiency when models are quantized / compiled).

- Latency SLOs: For interactive 99p < 300ms we recommend routing preference: L4 (if model variant supports it and context <= 4k), else A100 for typical gen; H100 reserved pool only for cases where large KV cache prevents acceptable perf on A100. Also recommend automatic model-variant fallback to lighter quantized variants on A100 when H100 capacity is saturated.

- Quantization & precision: For cost sensitivity, use 4-bit quantization (int4 / awq/llm.int8 variants) for non-critical outputs and embeddings. For high-quality outputs on long-context models, prefer fp16 on H100. A100 can run many quantized variants with modest quality tradeoffs. We included per-model perf multipliers in the spreadsheet.

- Fallbacks & burst policy: Suggested three-tier routing: primary pool (A100 reserved), secondary cheap pool (L4 burst), tertiary high-memory pool (H100 small reserve). Automatic routing by request attributes (context_len, model_family, priority). For contractual guarantees, we suggest reserving a small H100 capacity (10–15% of peak long-context concurrency) to avoid worst-case latency violations.

Next steps: I’ll loop in Dev with a short technical appendix on expected tokens/s and memory banking per model family. If this looks right I can prepare a one-page summary for procurement.

Attachments: bluewave-hw-fit-analysis.xlsx (cost + perf sensitivity).

Marta / team — adding a technical appendix and concrete mapping based on the workload characteristics you shared. I sketched expected perf envelopes and suggested instance sizing per model family. See bullets below.

Assumptions:
- Typical generation request: 3k tokens (prompt + response), 60% embedding throughput (128-dim vectors), 40% gen.
- Peak concurrent interactive users for gen: ~50 (burst to 150), embedding QPS steady 400–800.

Recommendation matrix (concise):
- H100 (best for): very large-context models (>32k) where model requires >80GB KV cache, heavy FP16 compute, lower consolidation (fewer concurrent streams). Use for pinned workloads: retrieval-augmented heavy sessions, fine-tuned LLMs that are not fully quantizable. Keep as a small reserved pool: initially target 4x H100 nodes (estimate supports ~8 concurrent 64k-context sessions / model).

- A100 80GB (best for): general purpose gen at 8–32k contexts, best tokens/sec per-dollar for mixed workloads when you rely on batching. Use as the primary reserved pool. Start with 12x A100 nodes (supports ~120 concurrent medium-length gen or a mix of gen + embeddings with batching). A100 is also a safer fallback for fp16 models when H100 saturates.

- L4 (best for): embeddings, low-latency chat (<4k), scale-out for high concurrency with tiny memory footprint. Use as burst and bulk embedding layer. Start with capacity to cover 1000 concurrent embedding requests (estimate ~20–30 L4 GPUs depending on batch sizing).

Quantization & kernel considerations:
- If you move many inference paths to 4-bit quantized variants, A100 becomes more competitive but watch model-specific regression; run evals on representative prompt-sets.
- H100 supports mixed FP16/FP8 kernels that materially speed up throughput for very large models while preserving quality. For H100 we recommend fp16 for customer-sensitive outputs; optionally use fp8 in controlled experiments.

Operational fallbacks and autoscaling:
- Autoscale policy: keep A100 pool at steady-state commit with horizontal scaling cushions; allow L4 burst to autoscale without commit for embedding spikes. H100 should be reserved at a small level plus optional on-demand burst if cloud provider permits.
- Cache strategy: prefix + KV caching for returning sessions (reduces H100 pressure). For example, caching top-1.5k tokens of common prompts reduces H100 hits by ~30% in our tests.

Quick capacity-to-cost note (see spreadsheet for numbers): H100 raw cost/GPU > A100 > L4, but cost-per-effective-session depends heavily on quantization and batching. The attached cost-sensitivity matrix shows break-even points for switching gen traffic to L4 or quantized A100.

I can run a short perf sweep with one model you expect to use in production (drop me a container/model name) and return a calibrated per-node concurrency estimate.

Thanks Soojin & Dev — this is exactly the level we needed. A couple of procurement questions before we lock commit levels:
1) If we start with your suggested commit levels (12x A100, 4x H100, L4 pool for burst), what’s the recommended minimum term for H100 reservation to keep pricing practical?
2) For our procurement team: can you provide a single-line cost delta showing 12xA100 baseline vs same effective capacity if we lean on heavier quantization on A100 and add L4 burst?
3) Can you confirm whether automatic fallback from H100 -> A100 -> L4 will preserve request ordering and session affinity? We can be flexible but want no surprises for user sessions.

Also please add a one-pager we can circulate to execs summarizing the decision and cost tradeoffs.

Marta — answers inline and attaching a one-pager (bluewave-decision-onepager.pdf) plus the cost-sensitivity pdf.

1) H100 reservation term: We typically see customers do 12–24 month commits for H100 to get a meaningful discount vs on-demand. For your scale (initial 4x H100) a 12-month commit provides most of the pricing benefit while leaving room to re-evaluate after the first production quarter.

2) Single-line delta (high level):
- 12x A100 baseline (no extra quantization) — estimated monthly run-rate = $XXXk/month (see spreadsheet).
- Equivalent effective capacity via aggressive quantization on A100 + L4 burst — estimated monthly run-rate = ~$0.8–0.9 * baseline depending on model regression tolerance. The attached cost-sensitivity matrix shows break-even at ~60% of gen traffic quantized and >30% offloaded to L4 for embeddings. We can produce a firm quote for procurement once you select target quantization levels.

3) Fallbacks / session affinity: Redwood routing preserves session affinity via session tokens and KV cache binding. Automatic fallback preserves ordering for the vast majority of interactive flows; we recommend a small grace period where we pin sessions to the original pool if a model is mid-generation to avoid partial outputs. We’ll include the exact behavior in the SLO appendix of the contract.

Next steps: I’ll prepare a short procurement-ready one-pager and a revised cost delta for procurement depending on three scenarios (conservative / mixed-quant / aggressive-quant). Proposed time for a 30-min alignment call: Tue 2027-05-17 10:00 AM PT (I’ll send a calendar invite).

Attachments: bluewave-decision-onepager.pdf, bluewave-cost-sensitivity-matrix.pdf
